title: Find it, and find it again from the other end

prereqs.why: This is the algorithm itself, written out rather than called.
Not found has to be reported somehow, and -1 is the convention this problem uses and the solution criticises.
The values are held in a vector and reached by index in both directions.

statement:
Implement the search yourself - do not call `std::find`, `index` or anything
equivalent.

Input is `n`, then `n` integers, then `q`, then `q` query values. For each query
print the **first** and **last** index at which it occurs, or that it is absent.
Indices are 0-based.

```
<query> first <i> last <j>
<query> absent
```

```
input:   6                   output:  4 first 1 last 4
         7 4 9 4 4 1                  7 first 0 last 0
         3                            5 absent
         4 7 5
```

### The point of the problem

Two functions, each a loop in one direction:

```cpp
int firstIndexOf(const std::vector<int>& v, int target);
int lastIndexOf(const std::vector<int>& v, int target);
```

Walking forwards and stopping at the first match is easy. Walking **backwards**
over an index that is unsigned is where this problem actually lives, and it is
the single most common source of silent memory bugs in C and C++. The solution
explains the two ways to write it safely.

### Boundary cases

A match at index 0 and a match at the last index. A value appearing exactly
once, so first and last are equal. An empty array, where every query is absent.
`q = 0`, which prints nothing. All elements identical. Negative values, which is
why `-1` as the not-found marker deserves a second look.

### Platform assumptions

Values and queries fit in a 32-bit `int`, `n` is at most 2000 and `q` at most
2000, so the simple O(n) per query is well inside the time limit. Indices fit in
an `int` because `n` is small; the solution says what to do when that is not
true.
hints: Forwards: `for (std::size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i)` and return `static_cast<int>(i)` on the first match. The cast is needed because `size()` is unsigned and the function returns `int`.

Backwards is the trap. `for (std::size_t i = v.size() - 1; i >= 0; --i)` never ends: `i >= 0` is always true for an unsigned type, and when `i` is 0 the `--i` wraps it to a huge number. The loop then reads far out of bounds.

Write the backward loop with a one-past-the-end counter instead: `for (std::size_t i = v.size(); i > 0; --i)` and look at `v[i - 1]`. The counter never goes below zero, and it stops cleanly on an empty vector.
